topic.subject: science
topic.title: Reproduction in plants
topic.scope: vegetative propagation, budding, spores, pollination, fertilisation, fruits and seeds, seed dispersal

misconceptions.statement: Plants can only grow from seeds.
misconceptions.why: Students primarily see seeds being planted in gardens or farms.
misconceptions.fix: Many plants can grow from vegetative parts like stems, roots, or leaves through asexual reproduction.

probe.question: If you plant a piece of a potato with an 'eye', will it grow into a plant?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because a potato is not a seed.

misconceptions.root_belief: only one way to do things

misconceptions.statement: The 'bud' in yeast is the same as a flower bud.
misconceptions.why: The same word is used for two different biological structures.
misconceptions.fix: A yeast bud is a small outgrowth that becomes a new individual, while a flower bud is an undeveloped shoot that will open into a flower.

probe.question: Does a yeast bud eventually open up into petals?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is a tiny flower waiting to bloom.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Spores are just very tiny seeds.
misconceptions.why: Both are small particles that lead to new plant-like growth.
misconceptions.fix: Spores are single-celled asexual units, whereas seeds are multi-cellular structures containing an embryo and food, resulting from sexual reproduction.

probe.question: Are spores produced by the fusion of male and female cells?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, like seeds, they need two parents.

misconceptions.root_belief: different things that look similar are the same

misconceptions.statement: Every flower has both male and female parts.
misconceptions.why: Common textbook diagrams often show bisexual flowers like Hibiscus.
misconceptions.fix: Some flowers, like corn or papaya, are unisexual and contain only stamens or only a pistil.

probe.question: Can a single flower have only stamens and no pistil?
probe.wrong_answer: No, a flower must have both to be a flower.

misconceptions.root_belief: all members of a group are identical

misconceptions.statement: Pollination and fertilisation are the same thing.
misconceptions.why: Both processes are closely linked in the reproductive cycle.
misconceptions.fix: Pollination is the transfer of pollen to the stigma, while fertilisation is the fusion of male and female gametes inside the ovary.

probe.question: Does fertilisation happen as soon as a bee touches a flower?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the bee fertilises the flower directly.

misconceptions.root_belief: sequential processes are a single event

misconceptions.statement: Insects visit flowers because they want to help the plant reproduce.
misconceptions.why: Students attribute human intentions to animals (anthropomorphism).
misconceptions.fix: Insects visit flowers to collect nectar or pollen for food; pollination is an accidental byproduct of their movement.

probe.question: Why does a bee carry pollen from one flower to another?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it knows the plant needs to make seeds.

misconceptions.statement: Fertilisation occurs on the surface of the stigma.
misconceptions.why: The stigma is where the pollen lands and is visible.
misconceptions.fix: Fertilisation occurs deep inside the ovary after the pollen tube grows down the style.

probe.question: Where do the male and female cells actually meet?
probe.wrong_answer: On the sticky top of the flower.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: Tomatoes and cucumbers are vegetables, not fruits.
misconceptions.why: Culinary definitions based on taste differ from botanical definitions.
misconceptions.fix: Botanically, any ripened ovary containing seeds is a fruit, including tomatoes, cucumbers, and ladyfingers.

probe.question: Is a cucumber a fruit or a vegetable in science?
probe.wrong_answer: A vegetable, because it is not sweet.

misconceptions.statement: Seeds are non-living objects because they don't move or breathe.
misconceptions.why: Seeds are dormant and show no visible signs of life.
misconceptions.fix: Seeds are living organisms in a state of dormancy; they respire slowly and contain a living embryo.

probe.question: Is a dry bean seed alive?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it only becomes alive when you water it.

misconceptions.root_belief: what is not moving is not alive

misconceptions.statement: Plants disperse seeds so that the 'baby' plants can see the world.
misconceptions.why: Teleological reasoning where students assign a purpose-driven 'why' to biological facts.
misconceptions.fix: Seed dispersal happens to prevent competition for sunlight and water between the parent and the offspring.

probe.question: Why is it important for seeds to fall far from the parent tree?
probe.wrong_answer: So they can find new friends and travel.

misconceptions.root_belief: biological structures exist for human-like purposes

misconceptions.statement: Pollen is the 'seed' of the flower.
misconceptions.why: Both are small grains involved in making new plants.
misconceptions.fix: Pollen contains male gametes; it must reach an egg to form a zygote, which then develops into a seed.

probe.question: If you plant pollen in the soil, will it grow into a plant?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because pollen is the plant's seed.

misconceptions.root_belief: different things that look similar are the same

misconceptions.statement: If you cut a living thing into pieces, it always dies.
misconceptions.why: Generalisation from higher animals (like humans or pets) where injury is fatal.
misconceptions.fix: In fragmentation, organisms like Spirogyra can break into pieces, and each piece grows into a new individual.

probe.question: What happens if an alga filament breaks into three parts?
probe.wrong_answer: The alga dies because it is broken.

misconceptions.root_belief: breaking a whole destroys its life
